summary: Project Objective: To eliminate the accessibility barriers that conventional climate crisis presentations and visual graphics pose for individuals who are blind or have low vision, and to foster an equitable, independent, and robust awareness regarding global warming and pollution. How the Problem Is Solved: This challenge has been addressed by developing a fully accessible and interactive website. The platform retrieves real-time data from NASA GISS and MERRA-2 open REST API endpoints, transforming increases in temperature and pollution into logarithmic frequency bands and acoustic textures that the human ear can clearly perceive. Furthermore, it ensures complete accessibility through full keyboard navigation, compatibility with screen readers (such as NVDA and VoiceOver), and adherence to WCAG 2.1 AA standards. Why It Matters: It guarantees scientific equity and inclusivity by ensuring that everyone can access climate data. Through psychoacoustic sound design, it translates the scale of the crisis into a tangible sense of urgency—a feeling that can be experienced mentally—thereby cultivating a profound level of social awareness. With its live data infrastructure and transparent mathematical models, it offers a high degree of technical reliability on an international scale.
details:
In project we did this Climate Sonification Jukebox is a NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 entry that lets people hear global warming instead of seeing it, making climate data accessible to visually impaired users. Temperature anomalies from 2000 to 2026 (+0.42 °C to +1.28 °C) are mapped to pitch using Weber–Fechner logarithmic scaling: 220 Hz rising to 1760 Hz, three octaves, with pitch doubling about every 8.7 years. Three ecological drivers each get their own timbre and range: fossil fuels (sawtooth, 180–1440 Hz), deforestation (triangle, 240–1200 Hz) and industrial pollution (square, 320–1920 Hz).

A synchronized graph cursor, a live year readout and an illustrated cat that overheats over time add visual context. A built-in voice narrates each sound, and the Listen and Read aloud tabs read their content line by line after seven seconds, with braille kept for embossers. Keyboard replay checks the last five key presses: sensible keys replay on R, random ones prompt “press any key three times.” Everything runs in one web page using the Web Audio API and speech synthesis.An this project impyrove my general intteligence.
